name: What Is Health and How Do We Stay Healthy?

scenes.animation: Zippy flexes tiny muscles in front of a mirror, wearing a 'Never Sick!' badge. Behind him, a phone screen glows at 2 a.m. and a pile of chips packets grows. Neo raises an eyebrow.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I haven't caught a cold all year. So I'm totally healthy, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not so fast. Being healthy is much more than just not falling sick.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.1 as a short comic strip: a Grade 8 boy in a new city sits alone, scrolls his phone, holds his head with headaches, lies awake at night. Then a doctor and a school counsellor help him make friends, and colour returns to the panels.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 3.1. A Grade 8 boy moved to a new city. With no friends and busy parents, he felt lonely and spent more time on social media.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He had headaches, lost weight and could not sleep. A doctor advised less screen time, and a counsellor helped him make friends.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So loneliness made his body sick too?

scenes.animation: A three-part circle builds: 'Physical', 'Mental', 'Social', joining into one ring labelled 'Health (WHO)'. A scroll unrolls with 'Ayurveda: dinacharya, ritucharya, prakriti'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. The World Health Organization defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ayurveda also teaches that true health is a balance of body, mind and surroundings, through daily and seasonal routines called dinacharya and ritucharya.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.2: two lists build side by side. Green 'Good habits': hygiene, balanced diet, exercise, relax or meditate. Red 'Harmful habits': too much screen time, daily junk food, sleeping late, skipping breakfast. Icons follow: fruits, cycling, yoga, a big 'NO' over tobacco and alcohol.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Activity 3.2, list your habits. Good ones: personal hygiene, a balanced diet, regular exercise, and time to relax.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Harmful ones: too much screen time, junk food every day, sleeping late, and skipping breakfast.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A healthy lifestyle means fruits, vegetables and whole grains, outdoor play, enough sleep, yoga or pranayama, and saying no to tobacco, alcohol and drugs.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.3: two playgrounds side by side, one clean with green grass, one littered with flies and mosquitoes buzzing. Then a smoky city street with an 'AQI' meter needle swinging into red; a cartoon child coughs. 'Exam Tip' sticker on the three-part circle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'd pick the clean playground. The other one is full of mosquitoes!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. People living in dirty surroundings may fall sick more often. Air pollution from vehicles and factories can cause coughing or asthma.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Air Quality Index, or AQI, tells us how clean the air is.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: when you write the WHO definition, include all three, physical, mental and social, plus 'not merely the absence of disease'.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a heart icon. Points: '1. Health = physical + mental + social well-being', '2. Healthy lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, no harmful substances', '3. Clean surroundings and good relationships matter'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a balanced diet, exercise, enough sleep and limited screen time keep us healthy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: clean surroundings, clean air and time with friends and family keep body and mind healthy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Phone down, cricket bat up!

name: Signs, Symptoms and Types of Diseases

scenes.animation: Zippy lies on a sofa with a thermometer in his mouth, dramatically groaning. The thermometer pops out and reads a high number. Neo holds a doctor's clipboard.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I feel terrible, Neo. My head hurts, and I'm so tired.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And your thermometer says fever. You just gave me one symptom and one sign.

scenes.animation: A split screen: left side 'Symptom: what you feel' shows pain, tiredness, dizziness inside a thought bubble; right side 'Sign: can be seen or measured' shows a thermometer, a rash, a blood pressure cuff and a swollen ankle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When we are unwell, something inside us is not working as it should.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A symptom is what we feel, like pain, tiredness or dizziness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A sign is something that can be seen or measured, like high body temperature, a rash, high blood pressure or swelling. Both help doctors understand what is wrong.

scenes.animation: A body outline with organs; one organ flickers red. Text: 'Disease: affects normal working of body or mind'. Cartoon pathogens march in: bacteria, virus, fungus, worm, protozoa, with a banner 'Pathogens'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A disease is a condition that affects the normal working of the body or mind. It can happen when organs or organ systems stop working properly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some diseases are caused by germs like bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms or protozoa. Disease-causing organisms are called pathogens.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Other diseases come from poor nutrition or an unhealthy lifestyle.

scenes.animation: Two big doors open. Door 1 'Communicable' shows germs jumping between people: typhoid, dengue, flu, chickenpox, COVID-19. Door 2 'Non-communicable' shows cancer, diabetes and asthma with a 'Does not spread' stamp, linked to icons of junk food, a sofa and smoke.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Diseases fall into two major types. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread from one person to another.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Examples are typhoid, dengue, flu, chickenpox and COVID-19.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Non-communicable diseases, like cancer, diabetes and asthma, are not caused by pathogens and do not spread. They are linked to lifestyle, diet or environment.

scenes.animation: A bar chart of India rises with a growing 'NCDs' bar labelled 'Most deaths in India today'. Icons of processed food, less exercise and a longer lifespan feed into it. 'Exam Tip' sticker on the words 'Symptom vs Sign'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So which kind is winning in India now?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Non-communicable diseases like diabetes, heart disease and cancer have become more common, because people eat more processed food, exercise less and live longer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Today, most deaths in India are caused by these NCDs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: pain is a symptom, but fever measured on a thermometer is a sign. Examiners love this difference.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a stethoscope icon. Points: '1. Symptom = felt; Sign = seen or measured', '2. Pathogens cause communicable diseases', '3. NCDs: not spread, linked to lifestyle; most deaths in India'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: a symptom is what we feel, a sign is what can be seen or measured.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and spread from person to person.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: non-communicable diseases do not spread, are linked to lifestyle, and cause most deaths in India.

name: How Communicable Diseases Spread and How to Stop Them

scenes.animation: A crowded school bus in winter. A boy sneezes and a cloud of cartoon germs bursts out, riding air currents to every seat. Zippy dives behind a backpack.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: One sneeze, and the whole bus is under attack!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's how many communicable diseases spread. Let's trace the routes.

scenes.animation: A route map like a metro diagram, built line by line from an 'Infected person' station: 'By air' (cough, sneeze), 'Direct contact' (handshake), 'Indirect contact' (shared towel), 'By food and water', 'Mosquitoes and houseflies: vectors', 'Rabid animal'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pathogens enter our body through the air we breathe, or through contaminated food and water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They spread through air when someone coughs or sneezes, by direct contact like shaking hands, or indirectly by sharing an infected person's things.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Insects like mosquitoes and houseflies also spread pathogens. Such insects are called vectors.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.4: Table 3.1 builds row by row in three coloured bands. Air: cold and flu (virus), chickenpox (virus), measles (virus), TB (bacteria, lungs). Water and food: hepatitis A (virus, liver), cholera and typhoid (bacteria, intestine), ascariasis (worms). Insects: malaria (protozoa), dengue (virus).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Activity 3.4, students listed common diseases. Through air: cold, flu, chickenpox and measles, all caused by viruses, and tuberculosis, caused by bacteria in the lungs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Through contaminated water and food: hepatitis A, a virus attacking the liver, and cholera and typhoid, caused by bacteria in the intestine.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Through insects: malaria, caused by protozoa, and dengue, caused by a virus.

scenes.animation: A roundworm cartoon curls inside an intestine, stealing food pellets, with the label 'Parasite: lives in or on another living being'. Then a mosquito net drops over a bed, and a bucket of still water gets tipped out.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Worms can live inside us? Gross!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Roundworms cause ascariasis. They feed on our nutrients and live as parasites, organisms that live in or on another living being.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For malaria and dengue, use mosquito nets and repellents, wear long-sleeved clothes, and stop mosquitoes breeding around your home.

scenes.animation: A checklist builds with ticks: soap handwash with bubbles, elbow-cough, mask in a crowd, own towel and handkerchief, boiled water on a stove, a sick child resting at home. 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Cholera, Typhoid, Hepatitis A = water-borne'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Simple precautions work. Wash hands with soap and water, cover your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze, and wear a mask in crowded places.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Don't share towels or handkerchiefs, keep food and water clean, and stay home to rest when unwell.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: if drinking water is contaminated, think of hepatitis A, cholera and typhoid. Tuberculosis and chickenpox spread through air.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a soap-bubble icon. Points: '1. Routes: air, contact, food and water, vectors', '2. Malaria = protozoa; TB, cholera, typhoid = bacteria', '3. Hygiene, masks, clean water, nets prevent spread'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: pathogens spread through air, contact, contaminated food and water, and vectors like mosquitoes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: malaria is caused by protozoa, while TB, cholera and typhoid are caused by bacteria.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: handwashing, covering coughs, clean water and mosquito nets stop the spread.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next bus ride, I'm sneezing into my elbow.

scenes.animation: Zippy hides behind a mask and sanitiser bottle from a sofa, a plate of samosas and a sugary cold drink. Neo shakes his head: 'Masks won't stop these.'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I've got my mask on. No disease can get me now!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A mask can't stop diabetes, Zippy. Some diseases don't come from germs at all.

scenes.animation: Three signposts point to non-communicable diseases: 'Lifestyle', 'Diet', 'Environment', leading to cancer, diabetes and asthma. A second branch shows Grade 6 deficiency diseases: 'Scurvy', 'Anaemia', 'Goitre' with an empty nutrient slot.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Non-communicable diseases like cancer, diabetes and asthma are linked to lifestyle, diet and environment. They are the most common cause of death in India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Diseases like scurvy, anaemia and goitre come from a lack of specific nutrients. These deficiency diseases are also non-communicable.

scenes.animation: A calendar flips past three months while a patient keeps visiting a clinic; label 'Chronic: more than 3 months'. Then diabetes causes stack as blocks: hormonal imbalance, unhealthy eating, lack of activity, being overweight.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Cancer, diabetes and asthma may last a long time, more than three months. These are called chronic diseases.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Diabetes is becoming common in adults and children. India now has one of the highest numbers of people with diabetes in the world.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It often develops from hormonal imbalance, unhealthy eating, lack of physical activity, and being overweight or obese.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.5: Zippy with a clipboard interviews a neighbourhood nurse and a grandparent. Table 3.2 fills in: 'Obesity: balanced diet and regular exercise', 'Diabetes: frequent urination, excessive thirst, weight loss, tiredness, slow healing', 'High blood pressure'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Activity 3.5, survey the three most common lifestyle diseases in your neighbourhood. Talk to a doctor, nurse, health worker or an informed family member.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For obesity, the suggested change is a balanced diet and regular exercise.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Diabetes shows frequent urination, excessive thirst, weight loss, tiredness and slow healing.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the cure starts in my own kitchen and playground.

scenes.animation: A portrait card: 'Kamal Ranadive (1917–2001), biomedical researcher'. Icons of tobacco, junk food and factory smoke link to 'Cancer risk'. 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Deficiency diseases are non-communicable'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Scientist Kamal Ranadive studied how hormones and certain viruses are linked to cancer. Her work showed that tobacco, diet and pollution raise cancer risk.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: scurvy, anaemia and goitre are non-communicable. Don't list them under infections.

scenes.animation: Recap board with an apple icon. Points: '1. NCDs: lifestyle, diet, environment', '2. Chronic = lasts more than 3 months', '3. Diabetes: rising in India; prevent with diet and activity'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: non-communicable diseases come from lifestyle, diet and environment, and include deficiency diseases.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: diseases lasting more than three months are called chronic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: diabetes is rising in India, and a balanced diet and exercise help prevent it.

scenes.animation: Two siblings in the same house during monsoon: one sneezes all week, the other plays happily. Zippy scratches his head between them.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Same house, same food. Why does only one of them keep falling sick?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because bodies differ in their ability to fight disease. But first, remember: prevention is better than cure.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.6: a map of Odisha zooms to Bhadrak district. Villagers build toilets; a chart of diarrhoea cases among children drops.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 3.6. In Bhadrak district, Odisha, a community sanitation campaign helped more people build and use toilets.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Open defecation fell, and children had fewer cases of diarrhoea and infections. Good sanitation greatly reduces communicable diseases.

scenes.animation: Inside the body: cartoon immune-system guards patrol. A vaccine drop enters; the guards study a 'wanted poster' of a harmless germ part, then instantly capture the real germ later. Labels: 'Immunity', 'Acquired immunity'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The natural ability of our body to fight disease is immunity. Our immune system does this job.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs. This gives acquired immunity, protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Vaccines are made from weakened or dead pathogens, or their harmless parts. A tetanus shot contains an inactivated bacterial toxin.

scenes.animation: Sepia 1700s English countryside: a milkmaid with cowpox blisters, Edward Jenner taking notes. A 'Think like a scientist' ladder builds: Observation, Hypothesis, Experiment, Result, Application. A graph line of countries reporting smallpox falls to zero at '1979: eradicated'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the late 1700s, English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not get smallpox.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He injected cowpox material into a boy, who later did not fall ill when exposed to smallpox. That was the first vaccine.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mass vaccination eventually helped eradicate smallpox worldwide.

scenes.animation: An Indian village scene of old: a teekedaar performs variolation. Then modern Indian vaccine factories ship boxes across a globe. A card: 'Maharaj Kishan Bhan: Rotavirus vaccine'. 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Vaccines = preventive, not curative'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India had an older method called variolation against smallpox, done by people called teekedaars. Today, India is one of the world's largest vaccine producers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Scientist Maharaj Kishan Bhan played a key role in developing the Rotavirus vaccine, which protects children from diarrhoea.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So if I'm already sick, I just take a vaccine?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Exam tip: vaccines are preventive, not curative. They don't treat someone who is already sick.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a shield icon. Points: '1. Sanitation prevents communicable diseases', '2. Vaccines train the immune system: acquired immunity', '3. Jenner: first vaccine; smallpox eradicated'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: good sanitation, like using toilets, prevents communicable diseases.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: vaccines train the immune system and give acquired immunity. They prevent, not cure.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, and vaccination wiped out smallpox.

scenes.animation: Zippy with a runny nose rushes to a chemist counter waving money: 'One antibiotic, please, fast!' The chemist shakes his head and points to a sign 'Prescription needed'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I have a cold. One antibiotic will fix it, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Stop right there. That's one of the biggest health mistakes people make.

scenes.animation: An antibiotic capsule targets a bacterium's unique parts and it pops. A virus and a protozoan stand unharmed as the capsule bounces off them. Label 'Antibiotics: bacteria only'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When our immune system fails, a doctor may give antibiotics, medicines that kill the bacteria causing a disease.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They target parts of bacterial cells that are different from human or animal cells.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So antibiotics do not work against viruses, like a cold, or diseases caused by protozoa.

scenes.animation: London, 1928: Alexander Fleming finds a discarded petri dish where a mould patch has a clear ring with no bacteria around it. A bottle labelled 'Penicillin: the first antibiotic' appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1928, Alexander Fleming, a bacteriologist from London, noticed a mould on a discarded petri dish that stopped bacteria from growing.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The mould released a substance that killed bacteria. This chance discovery gave us penicillin, the first antibiotic.

scenes.animation: Activity 3.7 infographic built step by step: a crowd of bacteria, a few coloured differently as 'resistant'; antibiotics wipe out the rest, including good bacteria; resistant ones multiply and pass resistance to others. Side panels show resistance spreading via hospitals, animal products and manure in fields.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity 3.7. Study how resistance develops. A few bacteria become resistant. Antibiotics kill the others, including good bacteria that protect us.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The resistant bacteria grow, take over, and pass resistance to other bacteria.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This is antibiotic resistance: bacteria once killed by an antibiotic now survive and multiply. It spreads through people, hospitals, animals and crops.

scenes.animation: A green rulebook opens: 'Only with a doctor's prescription', 'Correct dose', 'Right duration'. A farmer puts away an antibiotic injection for his cattle. Herbs and oils appear with 'Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani'. 'Exam Tip' sticker on 'Not for viral infections'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So use antibiotics wisely: only when prescribed by a doctor, in the correct dose and for the right duration. Don't give them to cattle unnecessarily either.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Traditional systems like Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani use herbs, oils and minerals, but may not work for all diseases at all stages.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Non-communicable diseases are managed with medicines, lifestyle changes and rehabilitation. Early diagnosis is key.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: asked why antibiotics are not given for cold or flu? Because these are viral, and antibiotics work only on bacteria.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a capsule icon. Points: '1. Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses', '2. Fleming, 1928: penicillin', '3. Misuse causes antibiotic resistance'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: antibiotics kill bacteria, but not viruses or protozoa.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: misusing antibiotics causes resistance, so take them only as a doctor prescribes.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Fine. Tissues and rest for my cold, then.
